Learning objectives & the big picture

  1. Discuss the assessment of pain.
  2. Differentiate acute and chronic pain.
  3. Interpret patient-selection considerations for acute and chronic pain.
  4. Discuss local analgesia and peripheral neuropathy.
  5. Apply the WHO pain ladder to clinical vignettes and select drug therapy.

Unifying model: Characterize the pain → locate the generator (inflammatory tissue, injured nerve, spinal modulation, central processing) → choose treatment matched to mechanism, severity, context and patient risk. A pain score informs the conversation; it does not substitute for functional assessment, examination, or safety review.

Objective 1 · Assess pain before choosing a drug

SOCRATES structures the interview: Site, Onset, Character, Radiation, Associations, Time course, Exacerbating/relieving factors, Severity. Ask how pain affects sleep, movement, function and goals, and reassess after treatment.

MUST KNOW

The professor explicitly warns against relying on vital signs, whether a patient “looks” distressed, whether a procedure “should” hurt, sleeping status, or assumptions that the patient will volunteer pain (slide 7).

RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · Can normal pulse and a sleeping patient exclude severe pain?

No. Neither is a reliable substitute for asking, examining, and reassessing pain.

Objective 2 · Acute versus chronic pain

DimensionAcuteChronic
Duration / causeShorter duration; lecturer uses <3–6 months; identifiable injury often presentMonths to years; mechanism may include altered nerve function and transmission
Biologic roleWarns of potentially harmful process; uncontrolled pain may trigger metabolic and hemodynamic changesPain may persist beyond tissue warning and involve nervous-system amplification
Associated featuresDistress sometimes visible; watch for atypical presentations in infants or dementiaSleep disruption and depression often coexist; outward distress may be absent
Treatment goalTreat cause and provide reliefImprove function, sleep and quality of life alongside relief
COMMON CONFUSION

Chronic pain is not “imaginary” if examination or imaging fails to show an active tissue lesion. The lecture contrasts pain presentation, not whether the pain is real.

RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · What is the major treatment-goal distinction in slide 9?

Acute: cure/treat cause; chronic: improve functionality. Both require relief and reassessment.

Objective 3 · Match drugs to the pain pathway

The lecture’s pathway begins with a peripheral noxious stimulus, the dorsal root ganglion, the dorsal horn, the ascending spinothalamic tract, the thalamus and cortex. A therapy can act at the injury site (NSAID), along the nerve (local anesthetic), in the spinal cord (epidural/local anesthetic, opioids), or centrally (opioids, ketamine and other modulators).

FOUNDATIONS LINK

Prostaglandins sensitise nociceptors; suppressing their synthesis reduces inflammatory pain. This is different from preventing a nerve action potential (local anesthesia) or dampening central neurotransmission (opioids).

Objective 3 · NSAIDs and patient selection

Mechanism: COX inhibition → decreased prostaglandins → less peripheral sensitization, pain and inflammation. The lecture emphasizes that relative COX-1/COX-2 selectivity helps predict GI, platelet and cardiovascular risks. Selecting an NSAID involves kidney function, peptic-ulcer/bleeding history, cardiovascular disease, pregnancy, other medications and duration.

AgentLecture-specific associationKey selection problem
AspirinAntiplatelet effect; used in cardiovascular diseaseSalicylate allergy, GI/bleeding risk; ibuprofen may interfere with low-dose aspirin effect
IbuprofenCommon for headache, dysmenorrhea, arthritis; slide notes IV form for PDA closureGI, renal and interactions; avoid undermining cardioprotective aspirin
NaproxenJoint pain, tendinitis, bursitis, dysmenorrheaCV and GI risk; lecture slide 15 comparison noted below
IndomethacinGout and ankylosing spondylitisRelatively high GI ulcer/bleed and CNS adverse effects
KetorolacPotent short-term NSAIDFive-day limit due to GI and renal toxicity
DiclofenacAvailable as patch and topical gelSystemic NSAID risks still matter with appropriate exposure
Meloxicam / piroxicamOA/RA; piroxicam more ulcerogenic per lectureRelative COX selectivity and GI risk differ
Etodolac / celecoxibCOX-2 preference/selectivity; lower GI injury in some settingsThrombotic/CV risk remains important
SOURCE CAUTION

Slide 15 states that naproxen has a higher cardiovascular-event risk than ibuprofen and that celecoxib exceeds nonselective NSAIDs. These comparisons are reproduced as lecture-specific statements, not universal current comparative-risk rankings.

RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · Which NSAID has a five-day maximum in this lecture, and why?

Ketorolac; limited due to renal and gastrointestinal toxicity.

Objective 4 · Local and regional anesthesia

Mechanism: Local anesthetics block voltage-gated Na⁺ channels → prevent propagated action potentials → reduce sensation in the affected nerve territory. Regional routes include local infiltration, peripheral nerve/plexus block, epidural and intrathecal approaches. Adding epinephrine promotes local vasoconstriction and can lower systemic absorption.

DrugDuration in lectureExamples / risk
Procaine; chloroprocaineShortPeripheral / epidural / regional uses
Tetracaine; mepivacaine; lidocaineIntermediateSpinal/procedure applications; lidocaine useful for topical and local infiltration
Bupivacaine; ropivacaineLongLabor epidural, nerve blocks and postoperative pain; bupivacaine flagged for highest toxicity risk
MUST KNOW

Local-anesthetic systemic toxicity can produce tinnitus, dizziness, agitation, seizures, respiratory arrest and cardiovascular depression, bradycardia, arrhythmias or arrest. These are safety signals, not expected therapeutic effects.

RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · What distinguishes a local anesthetic from an NSAID?

Local anesthetic blocks Na⁺ conduction; NSAID lowers prostaglandin synthesis.

Objective 3 · α₂ agonists and descending modulation

α₂ receptor stimulation reduces sympathetic neurotransmitter release and supports spinal/central antinociceptive modulation. The lecture identifies clonidine as an adjunct for cancer/postoperative pain and dexmedetomidine for postoperative pain. Both can cause hypotension; dexmedetomidine can cause bradyarrhythmias.

RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · Which two adverse effects should come to mind with dexmedetomidine?

Hypotension and bradyarrhythmia.

Objective 3 · Opioids, routes and safety

μ-opioid receptor (MOR) mechanism: Gi/Go-coupled receptor activation → inhibition of adenylyl cyclase, reduced presynaptic voltage-gated Ca²⁺ entry and enhanced K⁺ conductance → less excitatory transmitter release and reduced postsynaptic firing. The slides also list PLCβ/PKC signaling.

DrugLecture-specific pearl
CodeineMild–moderate; CYP2D6 prodrug
MorphineSevere pain; lecture labels it a drug of choice
FentanylSevere pain and anesthetic use; multiple transdermal/transmucosal/intranasal formulations
HydromorphoneMore potent; mentioned for PCA
HydrocodoneAcute/chronic severe pain; often combined with acetaminophen
MeperidineAcute severe pain and anesthetic-associated shivering
MethadoneChronic severe pain
SufentanilLabor analgesia with bupivacaine / general anesthesia
EXAM TRAP

The slide’s example PCA doses and monitoring intervals are educational examples, not a prescription or a universal order set. Patient-specific selection and monitoring are essential.

BOARD / CLINICAL ENRICHMENT

Important opioid safety concepts: sedation, respiratory depression, constipation, dependence, opioid-related overdose risk, and interactions with sedating medications. Consider multimodal and nonopioid strategies and monitor carefully.

RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · What changes at presynaptic and postsynaptic membranes after MOR activation?

Presynaptic Ca²⁺ entry decreases and postsynaptic K⁺ conductance increases, limiting nociceptive transmission.

Objective 3 · Ketamine and nonpharmacologic adjuncts

Ketamine antagonizes NMDA-mediated glutamatergic excitation and is described as a rapid-acting anesthetic producing profound analgesia. Dr. Winston notes intravenous bolus/infusion and its possible use as a morphine adjunct.

MSK CONNECTION

Modulating sensitization and pain processing matters particularly when pain persists beyond visible tissue injury. Different strategies may target peripheral inputs, spinal signaling and function.

Objective 4 · Peripheral neuropathic pain

Definition: Damage or dysfunction of peripheral nerves can impair sensory, motor or autonomic function and cause burning, shooting or tingling pain. Unlike a simple inflammatory process, nerve signaling and central amplification become major treatment targets.

Drug/classMechanism or roleLecture pearl
Amitriptyline / nortriptyline / desipramine (TCA)Increase synaptic monoamines involved in descending inhibitionAmitriptyline: anticholinergic/sedating; nortriptyline often fewer anticholinergic effects
Duloxetine / venlafaxine (SNRI)Increase serotonin and norepinephrine signalingDuloxetine also used in fibromyalgia; venlafaxine less ideal in hypertension per slide
Pregabalin / gabapentinBind the α₂δ subunit of presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels → reduce excitatory neurotransmissionDizziness, vertigo, confusion; pregabalin also used in fibromyalgia
Capsaicin (topical)TRPV1 activation followed by nociceptor desensitization/defunctionalizationLecture describes substance P depletion and modest relief
COMMON CONFUSION

TCAs/SNRIs, gabapentinoids and capsaicin do not act like COX-blocking NSAIDs; each addresses a different element of nerve-pain signaling.

RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · Which drug class binds the α₂δ subunit?

Gabapentinoids: pregabalin and gabapentin.

Objective 5 · Apply the pain ladder to cases

The professor teaches the WHO three-step ladder: Step 1 nonopioid ± adjuncts for mild pain; Step 2 a weak opioid (the lecture cites codeine and some combinations) for persisting/moderate pain; Step 3 a strong opioid for severe pain. For severe acute pain, urgent appropriately monitored treatment may begin at a higher step rather than waiting for every earlier step.

Case A · Ankylosing spondylitis (slides 44–45)

Twenty-year-old with >3 months inflammatory-pattern low-back stiffness, improvement with activity, nocturnal symptoms and iritis. The lecturer’s options point to ibuprofen: it treats the inflammatory generator rather than merely suppressing pain centrally.

Case B · Sickle-cell vaso-occlusive crisis (slides 46–47)

Twenty-two-year-old reports 9/10 diffuse pain despite home hydrocodone/acetaminophen. Among the lecture options, morphine best matches severe acute pain and inadequate home treatment. Assess and monitor closely; use patient-specific crisis management pathways.

RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · Why is ibuprofen favored over morphine in the first case?

The clinical pattern is inflammatory axial pain; an NSAID treats inflammatory prostaglandin signaling and is an appropriate initial lecture choice.

RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · Why is morphine favored in the second case?

Severe acute vaso-occlusive pain despite prior home analgesics warrants prompt appropriately monitored strong analgesia.

MASTER THESE BEFORE MOVING ON

  1. Assessment precedes drug: SOCRATES + pain scale + function, without using appearance or vitals as exclusion tests.
  2. Acute ≠ chronic: goals and mechanisms differ, even though both require relief and respect for reported pain.
  3. Know the anatomic target: COX at inflammation, Na⁺ channels in the peripheral nerve, MOR and α₂ within neural pathways, NMDA for excitation.
  4. Choose by risk: NSAID renal/GI/CV risk, local-anesthetic cardiotoxicity, opioid sedation/respiratory risk.
  5. Match mechanism to vignette: inflammatory axial pain → NSAID; severe vaso-occlusive episode → monitored strong analgesia.

THE MOST USEFUL FIRST AID CONNECTIONS

FIRST AID CONNECTION: (1) μ-opioid Gi signaling predicts reduced transmitter release; (2) local anesthetic Na⁺ blockade prevents conduction; (3) TCA/SNRI augment descending inhibitory monoamines; (4) gabapentinoids bind α₂δ Ca²⁺ channel subunits; (5) NMDA antagonism limits excitatory transmission. These reinforce lecture mechanisms rather than expand to an unrelated pain-pharmacology chapter.
